```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 5.5, dpi = 80)
library(cytokineR)
library(data.table)
```

There is no single best way to pre-process multiplex cytokine data: it depends
on the kit, the instrument, the plate layout and what was put on every plate.
cytokineR therefore treats the choice as an experiment. You describe candidate
pipelines, and `benchmark_pipelines()` scores them on your own data.

Three ingredients make the comparison meaningful.

## 1. Material that should give the same answer

Without knowing the true concentrations, the best evidence is material that
was measured more than once: control materials on every plate, replicate
wells, and samples re-measured in several batches ("bridging samples"). A good
pipeline makes repeated measurements of the same material agree -- *without*
erasing the differences between study samples.

## 2. Metrics that do not depend on the scale

Pipelines produce different scales (log2 FI, multiples of blank,
concentrations), so raw SDs or CVs are not comparable. All metrics are
scale-free:

| metric | meaning | better |
|---|---|---|
| `reliability_plate` | 1 - (technical variance of repeated material across plates) / (variance of the study samples) | higher |
| `reliability_batch` | the same across batches | higher |
| `plate_r2` | adjusted partial R^2 of plate among study samples (within strata) | lower (for randomised layouts) |
| `bio_r2` | adjusted partial R^2 of known biology, e.g. time point within subject | higher |
| `detected` | fraction of study-sample values that are quantified, not censored | higher |
| `truth_rho`, `truth_rmse` | agreement with the true concentrations (simulations only) | higher / lower |

`reliability` is a signal-to-noise ratio (an intra-class correlation): it is
1 when repeats agree perfectly and 0 when technical noise is as large as the
whole spread of the study. `bio_r2` guards against over-correction: a method
that flattens everything would score well on agreement but lose biology.
`detected` guards against imputation hiding problems.

## 3. Hold-out: never grade a method on what it was fitted to

If a pipeline anchors every plate to control *A*, control *A* will agree
perfectly across plates by construction -- that says nothing about the
samples. `benchmark_pipelines(holdout = ...)` therefore sets
`use_for_fit = FALSE` for the held-out material before each pipeline runs (no
method may use it for estimation) and computes the reliability metrics on
exactly that material.

## A first benchmark

`expand_pipelines()` builds every combination of the alternatives per stage:

```{r}
grid <- expand_pipelines(
  signal = list(log2 = pipe_transform("log2"),
                MoB  = pipe_transform("mob"),
                MoS  = pipe_transform("mos", by_conc = TRUE)),
  plate  = list(none   = NULL,
                median = pipe_normalize("median", within = "time"),
                ctrl   = pipe_normalize("anchor", anchors = "ctrl_low",
                                        scope = "batch")),
  batch  = list(none = NULL, bridge = pipe_correct_batch("bridge"))
)
length(grid)
head(names(grid))
```

Add some concentration-based strategies:

```{r}
conc <- list(
  "5PL/plate > Tobit > bridge" =
    cyto_pipeline(pipe_calibrate("5pl"), pipe_impute("tobit"),
                  pipe_correct_batch("bridge")),
  "shared 5PL > rank-Tobit > bridge" =
    cyto_pipeline(pipe_calibrate("shared"), pipe_impute("rank_tobit"),
                  pipe_correct_batch("bridge")),
  "harmonise > one curve > rank-Tobit" =
    cyto_pipeline(pipe_transform("log2"),
                  pipe_normalize("anchor", anchors = "standard",
                                 scope = "batch", fit = "affine"),
                  pipe_correct_batch("bridge"),
                  pipe_calibrate("5pl", curve_by = NULL,
                                 standards = ~ batch == "1"),
                  pipe_impute("rank_tobit"))
)
```

Run them, holding out the high control (the low control may be used as an
anchor):

```{r}
bm <- benchmark_pipelines(cyto_example, c(grid, conc), holdout = "ctrl_high",
                          metrics = default_metrics(bio = ~ time,
                                                    adjust = ~ subject),
                          verbose = FALSE)
bm$summary[1:10, .(pipeline,
                   rel_plate = round(reliability_plate, 3),
                   rel_batch = round(reliability_batch, 3),
                   plate_r2 = round(plate_r2, 3),
                   bio_r2 = round(bio_r2, 3),
                   detected = round(detected, 2),
                   mean_rank)]
```

Each point below is one analyte; the diamond is the mean.

```{r, fig.height = 7}
top <- bm$summary$pipeline[c(1:6, nrow(bm$summary) - 0:1)]
bm_top <- bm
bm_top$results <- bm$results[pipeline %in% top & metric != "truth_rmse"]
bm_top$summary <- bm$summary[pipeline %in% top]
plot(bm_top)
```

### Cross-fitting

With several kinds of repeated material, hold each out in turn. Bridging
samples are usually the only anchor between batches, so they are split into
folds with `holdout_folds()`: the batch correction is fitted on half of them
and judged on the other half.

```{r}
folds <- c(list(high_ctrl = "ctrl_high"),
           holdout_folds(cyto_example, "bridge", k = 2, prefix = "bridges_"))
lengths(folds)
cf <- benchmark_pipelines(cyto_example, grid[c("log2 > ctrl", "log2 > ctrl > bridge",
                                               "MoB > median > bridge",
                                               "MoS > bridge")],
                          holdout = folds, verbose = FALSE)
cf$results[metric == "reliability_batch",
           .(reliability_batch = round(mean(value), 3)), by = .(fold, pipeline)]
```

On the held-out bridging samples, the pipeline without batch correction is
clearly worse -- evidence that the bridge correction generalises to samples
it was not fitted on.

## Developing methods against the truth

Real data cannot tell you *why* a method fails. `simulate_cyto()` generates
studies with known concentrations under a physical model of plate effects
(gain, potency, background), kit-lot errors, bad standard wells and low
abundance, and `benchmark_simulations()` runs pipelines over scenarios:

```{r}
pipes <- c(grid[c("log2", "log2 > median > bridge", "MoB > bridge",
                  "log2 > ctrl > bridge")], conc[c(1, 2)])
scen <- list(default = list(plates_per_batch = 3),
             bad_standards = list(plates_per_batch = 3,
                                  bad_standard_prob = 0.15),
             confounded = list(plates_per_batch = 3, design = "by_time"))
bs <- benchmark_simulations(pipes, scen, reps = 1, verbose = FALSE)
plot(bs, metric = "truth_rho")
```

A larger study (6 scenarios, 5 data sets each, 11 pipelines) is in
`system.file("scripts", "simulation_study.R", package = "cytokineR")`.
Conclusions from simulations are only as good as the simulator's model, so
use them to generate hypotheses and to debug methods, and confirm on real
data with hold-out material.

## Designing plates so that methods can be compared

The benchmark can only be as good as the repeated material on the plates. For
studies run with cytokineR in mind:

* **A pooled control on every plate**, in duplicate, ideally at two levels
  (a pool of study-like samples, plus a spiked or concentrated pool). One can
  serve as anchor and the other as hold-out.
* **Bridging samples** when the study spans several kit lots or runs:
  8--10 study samples re-measured in every batch, covering the range of
  concentrations.
* **Randomised layout** across plates (stratified by group and time point),
  so that sample-based normalisation and `plate_r2` are meaningful.
* **Standards and blanks in duplicate** on every plate, and the lot-specific
  assigned concentrations recorded per batch.
* **Named wells** in the instrument software, so that sample ids survive the
  export.
